call_overview.title: About the call
call_overview.question: What does the call offer, and who can apply?

cards.title: What the call wants
cards.question: What is the principal thing the project must develop, and which problem or need must it address?
cards.answer:
Inland vessels that sail partly or fully emission-free or climate-neutral, through the purchase and installation of a new energy line (the engines and on-board systems that power at least the propulsion) on a newbuild or retrofitted ship.
The subsidy covers five kinds of energy line, each with its own budget:
- Battery-electric: 100% electric final drive powered by fixed or swappable batteries that can deliver at least 70% of the ship's energy need (average daily need, or the need between two charging or swap moments on a fixed route).
- Fuel-cell electric: 100% electric final drive powered by a hydrogen fuel-cell system that can deliver at least 70% of the energy need.
- Methanol: a combustion engine that can run at least 50% on methanol; retrofit only.
- Hydrogen combustion: a combustion engine that can run at least 50% on hydrogen.
- Hybrid-electric: an electric drive of at least 50% of the installed power plus a battery for at least 3 hours at full electric power or 50% of the energy need, chargeable on shore; retrofit of small ships only (waterways of CEMT class I to III, the European classes for small and shallow waterways).
Optionally, and only together with an energy line, the project may include shore-side charging or fuelling infrastructure the ship needs for its propulsion: charging points at a terminal, a crane to swap battery or hydrogen containers, or changes to a bunker station for green hydrogen or methanol. Shore power that only serves the ship's needs at the quay (the hotel function) is excluded; upgrading existing shore power to higher capacity so that propulsion batteries can be charged is allowed.
The need comes from the sector and national climate policy: the Netherlands has committed to a climate-neutral and almost emission-free inland shipping fleet by 2050, but cleaner propulsion still has an unprofitable gap in 2026–2030 because renewable energy carriers cost more than diesel, so shipowners hold back investment. Applicants for hydrogen or methanol must explain why they did not choose a battery or fuel-cell electric energy line.

cards.title: Project impact
cards.question: Which wider system outcomes and impacts must the project support?
cards.answer:
Each funded ship must cut its CO2 emissions: after the project it must at least qualify as a clean inland vessel, and projects that cut more CO2 per euro of subsidy rank higher.
- Clean vessel: a cargo ship must emit at least 50% less CO2 per tonne-kilometre than the EU reference value for heavy trucks; a passenger ship must take at least 50% of its energy from CO2-free fuel or plug-in power, as defined in the EU General Block Exemption Regulation (the EU state-aid rules the scheme uses).
- Zero-emission vessel: a ship with no CO2 from its exhaust, so no diesel engine or generator on board; it earns 10 percentage points more subsidy.
- Targets behind the scheme: about 150 to 160 ships made cleaner over 2026–2029, a structural reduction of 0.11–0.14 million tonnes of CO2 a year from 2032, and the national goal of 150 emission-free ships in service by 2030.
- Other aims: share operational knowledge, create front-runners for different ship types and sailing profiles, serve a variety of entrepreneurs, contribute to the roll-out of shore infrastructure, and cut nitrogen and particulate emissions, especially from small ships that sail in towns and near Natura 2000 nature areas.
The scheme follows the national energy system plan's line 'doe elektrisch wat elektrisch kan' (electrify whatever can be electrified): most of the budget is reserved for battery and fuel-cell electric energy lines.

cards.title: Who it suits
cards.question: Who may lead, which partners must take part, and how must the work be shared?
cards.answer:
Dutch inland shipping companies that operate, or will operate, a commercial inland vessel; port operators and energy suppliers can join only for the shore infrastructure.
- Lead applicant: a Dutch inland shipping entrepreneur (Nederlandse binnenvaartondernemer), meaning a company with a main or branch establishment in the Netherlands that operates the ship or will operate it after the project. Fishing vessels and recreational craft are excluded. The company may not be in financial difficulty.
- Partners: none for an energy line alone. A request that includes charging or fuelling infrastructure must come from a consortium (samenwerkingsverband) whose lead (penvoerder, the party that applies on behalf of all) is the shipping entrepreneur; the regulation gives a port operator or an energy supplier as examples of partners.
- Distribution of work and funding: each consortium participant that receives subsidy counts as an applicant and must request at least EUR 150,000; the consortium agreement must reach RVO (Netherlands Enterprise Agency, which runs the scheme) within 8 weeks of the grant decision.
- Limits: one energy line on one ship per application, and at most four applications per entrepreneur, or per group of related companies, per opening.
- Suits best: owners of cargo, passenger, ferry and work vessels planning a newbuild or retrofit, together with shipyards, propulsion and battery suppliers as their contractors, and port, terminal or energy companies that would own the shore infrastructure.

cards.title: Innovation
cards.question: How new must the project be, and in what must it innovate?
cards.answer:
No new technology is required: the scheme funds the early scale-up of propulsion techniques that have just passed the demonstration stage.
Innovative, not yet demonstrated techniques at a lower technology readiness level are explicitly not eligible; they belong in other schemes such as the Maritiem Masterplan (a Dutch subsidy for maritime demonstration projects at TRL 5–7). The innovation for the shipowner lies in the system on board (a new energy line with batteries, fuel cells or hydrogen or methanol engines) and, optionally, in the shore infrastructure that supplies it.
cards.sources: Staatscourant 2026, 33019 (Tijdelijke subsidieregeling vroege opschaling energietransitie binnenschepen 2026–2029) · Toelichting § 2.3 Toelichting: géén onderdeel van de subsidieregeling; § 3.3.1 Maritiem Masterplan

cards.title: Maturity
cards.question: Which maturity level is expected at the start and end of the project?
cards.answer:
TRL 8–9 (technology proven and ready for commercial use), the stage the scheme calls 'vroege opschaling' (early scale-up).
The regulation notes that at the first opening no Stage V certified (meeting the EU emission standard for such engines) methanol or hydrogen combustion engines are yet on the market, so it expects those energy lines to be requested mainly in later openings.
cards.sources: Staatscourant 2026, 33019 (Tijdelijke subsidieregeling vroege opschaling energietransitie binnenschepen 2026–2029) · Toelichting § 2.3; § 2.1.2 Energielijn methanol; § 2.1.3 Energielijn waterstof

cards.title: Demonstration and integration of work
cards.question: Where must the solution be demonstrated, and how must the work fit with existing systems?
cards.answer:
The energy line is not demonstrated but installed on a working ship that sails commercially, and its fuel supply must fit the ship's real sailing profile.
- The applicant must show, with a realistic sailing profile, how often, where and by whom the ship will be charged or fuelled, and how the share of fossil and renewable energy develops; agreements with shippers, energy suppliers or terminals strengthen the case.
- Funded shore infrastructure must be open to interested users on equal, non-discriminatory market terms, and shared infrastructure scores higher than infrastructure for a few ships.
- Funded hydrogen fuelling points must supply only renewable hydrogen, and methanol points only renewable methanol of non-biological origin, by 31 December 2035.
- Hybrid-electric batteries must be chargeable on shore.

call_overview.title: Relevance to TenneT
call_overview.question: Why is this call relevant to TenneT?

cards.title: Why it matters to TenneT
cards.question: Why does this call matter to TenneT, and why can't TenneT take part itself?
cards.answer:
The scheme puts battery-electric ships and their shore charging points into Dutch ports and waterways, a new and partly flexible electricity demand on the grid.
Our judgement: most of the budget goes to battery and fuel-cell electric propulsion and up to EUR 10 million to shore charging, battery-swap and bunkering points, which add charging loads and battery capacity at ports and terminals. This is close to TenneT's work on congestion forecasts for electric-vehicle charging (Grids and Benefits) and on time-dependent grid access for batteries; swappable ship batteries charged on shore could in time become flexible demand, though the call does not say so. TenneT could use knowledge from the funded projects, which recipients must help share, to anticipate charging demand in port areas. TenneT cannot take part itself: only a Dutch inland shipping entrepreneur may apply, and the shore infrastructure consortium must be led by one, with the regulation naming port operators and energy suppliers as partners and setting out no role for a grid operator.

funding_timing_submission.title: Funding
funding_timing_submission.question: How much funding can the project receive?

cards.title: Funding envelope
cards.answer:
EUR 36,928,300 for the 2026 opening, split into fixed budgets per energy line, out of EUR 231.2 million for the scheme's four yearly openings (2026–2029).
- Budgets in the 2026 opening: battery-electric EUR 8,108,620; fuel-cell electric EUR 8,108,620; methanol EUR 2,027,155; hydrogen combustion EUR 2,027,155; hybrid-electric EUR 6,656,750; charging and fuelling infrastructure EUR 10,000,000. Money left in one energy line may go to the next-ranked projects in the battery-electric, then fuel-cell, hydrogen and methanol lines, not to infrastructure or hybrid-electric.
- Grant request: per ship at most EUR 800,000 for battery-electric (EUR 2.5 million if the batteries are bought within the application), EUR 3 million for fuel-cell electric, EUR 1.5 million for methanol, EUR 1.5 million for hydrogen combustion and EUR 500,000 for hybrid-electric, plus up to EUR 600,000 for the infrastructure; at least EUR 150,000 per applicant per project.
- Total project size: not capped; the eligible costs are the extra cost over a conventional ship for a newbuild, or the full cost of the new energy line for a retrofit.
- Funding form: an investment subsidy on actual eligible costs.

cards.title: Funding rate and co-financing
cards.answer:
The energy line is funded at up to 50% of eligible costs for a large company and the shore infrastructure at up to 40%; the applicant pays the rest.
- Energy line, large company: 50%; medium-sized company: 60%; small company: 70%.
- Zero-emission bonus: plus 10 percentage points for the energy line if the ship qualifies as zero-emission after the project (no diesel engine or generator on board), for example 60% for a large company.
- Charging or fuelling infrastructure: 40% for every applicant, with no increase.
- Co-financing conditions: no other subsidy may have been granted for the same activities, and aid may not be combined beyond the EU state-aid limits; the project plan must explain how the own share is financed, and bank or investor commitments may be attached.

cards.title: Budget constraints
cards.answer:
Only the investment in the energy line and the shore infrastructure is eligible; operating costs such as fuel or electricity are not.
- Eligible costs: for a newbuild, the extra cost of the new energy line over a conventional ship of the same category with a Stage V diesel engine (shown with reference quotes); for a retrofit, the cost of buying and installing the new energy line, including on-board tanks, piping, charging connections, safety changes and batteries or tank containers that are bought or financially leased.
- Caps: in a retrofit, an engine is eligible only up to the currently installed power.
- Excluded costs: operating costs; rented or operationally leased batteries; a diesel engine kept alongside a battery-electric line; shore power that only serves the ship at the quay.
- Hourly rates: where used, by full-cost accounting, by cost per unit plus a fixed 50% for indirect costs, or at a fixed EUR 80 an hour.
cards.sources: Staatscourant 2026, 33019 (Tijdelijke subsidieregeling vroege opschaling energietransitie binnenschepen 2026–2029) · Artikel 4; Artikel 5 Standaardberekeningswijze uurtarieven; Toelichting § 2.3 (Operationele uitgaven); Artikelsgewijs deel, Artikel 3 en Artikel 4 (Meerkosten, Retrofit, Noodzakelijke voorzieningen aan boord, Laad- en tankinfrastructuur)

cards.title: Cash flow and financial exposure
cards.answer:
Up to 80% of the grant is paid in advance, so the shipowner pre-finances only the last 20% until the grant is settled.
- Payment model: 30% advance within 2 weeks of the grant decision; 50% at the start of the project (when the main component, such as the battery pack or engine, arrives at the shipyard, or work on the shore infrastructure starts), possibly in the calendar year after the start; the rest after the final settlement.
- Financial reporting or audit: no auditor's statement is needed at settlement, but invoices and proof of payment for all costs must be supplied.

funding_timing_submission.title: Timing
funding_timing_submission.question: What timing should the proposal submission and project follow?

cards.title: Application route
cards.answer:
One stage: a tender (all complete applications received by the deadline are ranked together, so the order of submission does not matter), online through RVO with eHerkenning level 3 (the Dutch business login).
- Stage 1 — Application: from 17 November 2026, 09:00, to 16 March 2027, 17:00. An application that includes charging or fuelling infrastructure starts with the energy-line application, which must be completed first, followed by a separate infrastructure application.
- Additional procedure: RVO holds information sessions on 3 December 2026 (on location) and 8 December 2026 (online). Later openings in 2027–2029 get new periods and budgets, announced in the Staatscourant (the Dutch government gazette).
cards.sources:
Staatscourant 2026, 33019 (Tijdelijke subsidieregeling vroege opschaling energietransitie binnenschepen 2026–2029) · Artikel 9, achtste en negende lid; Artikel 6, derde lid

cards.title: Project window
cards.answer:
A project must start within 12 months of the grant decision and end within 2 years (retrofit) or 3 years (newbuild) of that decision.
- Maximum duration: 24 months from the grant decision for a retrofit, 36 months for a newbuild.
- Required start: work may not start before the application is submitted, or the application is rejected; the project counts as started when the main component of the energy line arrives at the shipyard or work on the shore infrastructure begins, which must happen within 12 months of the grant decision.
- Completion deadline: the end date set in the grant decision; the request for final settlement is due within 13 weeks of completion.

cards.title: Decision and contracting
cards.answer:
RVO decides as soon as possible and at the latest within 13 weeks of the tender closing, so by mid-June 2027.
- Funding decision: within 13 weeks after 16 March 2027.
- Conditions before starting: with charging or fuelling infrastructure, the signed consortium agreement must reach RVO within 8 weeks of the grant decision. A grant may be given under a budget reservation (subject to parliament approving the budget).

funding_timing_submission.title: Application
funding_timing_submission.question: Mandatory information to include in the application

cards.title: Mandatory submission package — pass/fail
cards.answer:
An application without the RVO formats for the project plan and the two CO2 calculations is not accepted.
- Application form: RVO's online form; project plan only in the RVO format, at most 20 pages in Verdana 9 point, with a public summary of at most three quarters of a page.
- Budget: a substantiated budget in the RVO format; quotes (provisional quotes up to 6 months old allowed) that contain no irrevocable commitments yet.
- Mandatory annexes: two CO2 calculations in RVO's Excel format (maximum-use potential and expected use); a calculation showing the ship will be a clean or zero-emission vessel; proof of ship ownership or of the newbuild order; the full certificate of inspection of the ship (for a retrofit); last year's sailing-time log; an SME declaration or, for a large company, a declaration of incentive effect; the 'not a company in difficulty' declaration and decision scheme with the latest annual reports signed by an accountant.
- Partner documents: with shore infrastructure, the details of each consortium participant, the location of the infrastructure, and the consortium agreement after the decision.
- Registration: eHerkenning level 3.

cards.title: Evaluation and selection — scored or ranked
cards.answer:
Applications are ranked per energy line on four criteria worth 100 points, and the budget of each line goes to the highest scores.
- Criterion A, up to 40 points: maximum CO2 reduction (tank-to-wake, from the ship's own exhaust) the energy line can achieve over 10 years per euro of subsidy for the energy line, from RVO's calculation format.
- Criterion B, up to 30 points: the CO2 reduction from the expected actual use over 10 years per euro of subsidy, for example if the ship still sails partly on diesel until charging or bunkering becomes available.
- Criterion C, up to 15 points: how well A and B are substantiated, for example by chain cooperation, agreements with shippers, energy suppliers or terminals, and a sound business case.
- Criterion D, up to 15 points: quality of the plan, budget and planning, and, with shore infrastructure, how widely it is accessible to third parties.
- Thresholds: at least 8 points on C and at least 8 on D, or the application is rejected.
- Ranking rules: equal scores are decided by lot; the infrastructure subsidy is left out of the per-euro calculations of A and B.

cards.title: Conditional and exceptional requirements
cards.answer:
Hydrogen and methanol applicants must justify not choosing electric propulsion, and a few conditions apply after the grant.
- Conditional — hydrogen or methanol combustion engine: the application must explain why a battery or fuel-cell electric energy line was not chosen.
- Conditional — shore infrastructure: apply in a consortium led by the shipping entrepreneur and submit the consortium agreement within 8 weeks of the decision, or the infrastructure cannot be funded under the rules.
- Conditional — after the grant: an annual progress report during the project, and from the grant decision to 5 years after settlement cooperation in sharing non-confidential results, such as the charging location and its total power, and in the scheme's evaluation.
- Exception — grant over EUR 100,000: the recipient's name, company size, sector and amount are published on the EU State Aid Transparency website.
- Recommended: attend an RVO information session on 3 or 8 December 2026.
